en: Thus have I heard: Majjhima Nikāya 105, the Sunakkhatta Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood in the Gabled Hall.
Now on that occasion, a number of bhikkhus had declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
"We understand: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'"
Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son heard:
“It seems that many bhikkhus have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’”
Then Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, said this to the Blessed One:
“I have heard this, Bhante:”
“It is said, Bhante, that many bhikkhus have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One, saying:
‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
As for those bhikkhus, Bhante, who have declared final knowledge in the presence of the Blessed One:”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—
did those bhikkhus, Bhante, declare final knowledge rightly, or were some among them declaring final knowledge out of overestimation?
“Sunakkhatta, those bhikkhus who declared final knowledge in my presence:”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—thus they understand.
Among them, Sunakkhatta, some bhikkhus have rightly declared final knowledge, while others here have declared final knowledge out of overestimation.
In that regard, Sunakkhatta, for those bhikkhus who have rightly declared final knowledge, it is exactly so.
But regarding those monks who, out of overestimation, declared final knowledge there, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata thus:
‘I shall teach the Dhamma to them.
And so, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata in this matter:
‘I shall teach them the Dhamma.
Yet even so, Sunakkhatta, there are certain foolish men here who, having repeatedly formulated questions, approach the Tathāgata and ask them.
In that regard, Sunakkhatta, it occurs to the Tathāgata thus:
“‘I shall teach them the Dhamma,’ yet even for him there is change.
“Now is the time, Blessed One;
now is the time, Sublime One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
“In that case, Sunakkhatta, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"There are, Sunakkhatta, these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure,
and provocative of lust— these, Sunakkhatta, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
It is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some person here might be intent upon worldly material things.

For a person, Sunakkhatta, who is intent upon worldly gain, conversation that accords with that [gain] is established for him; he reflects upon it and deliberates upon it in accordance with its nature; he associates with such a person and finds satisfaction therein.

But when conversation connected with the imperturbable (*āneñja*) is being held, he does not wish to hear it, he does not lend an ear, he does not apply his mind to understand it, he does not associate with such a person, and he does not find satisfaction therein.
"Just as if, Sunakkhatta, a man had been long away from his own village or town,
and he were to see another man who had recently departed from that village or town;
he would ask that man about the safety, the abundance of food, and the health of that village or town."
Suppose that man were to describe to him the security, abundance of food, and freedom from disease of that village or town.
What do you think, Sunakkhatta,
would that man listen to him with eager ears, lend an attentive ear, set his mind on understanding, associate with that man, and find satisfaction in him?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that here some person might be intent on worldly gain.

For a person intent on worldly gain, Sunakkhatta, conversation suited to that state arises; he reflects and ponders in accordance with it, he associates with such a person, and he finds satisfaction in that.

Furthermore, when a discourse connected with the imperturbable is being delivered, he does not wish to hear it, does not lend an ear, does not apply his mind to understand it, does not associate with that person, and does not find satisfaction in it.
Of such a person, it should be known:
"This individual is dissociated from the fetter of the imperturbable, for he is intent upon worldly gain."
"It is indeed possible, Sunakkhatta, that here a certain person might be intent upon the imperturbable (*āneñja*).

For a person intent upon the imperturbable, Sunakkhatta, conversation appropriate to it arises; he reflects and deliberates in accordance with its nature, associates with such a person, and finds satisfaction therein."

Furthermore, when talk associated with worldly gain is being delivered, he does not wish to hear it, he does not lend an ear, he does not set his mind on understanding it, he does not associate with that person,
and he finds no satisfaction in it. Just as, Sunakkhatta, a withered leaf fallen from its stem is incapable of becoming green again,
even so, Sunakkhatta, for a person whose mind is intent upon the imperturbable (āneñja), those fetters of worldly gain have fallen away.
Thus he should be understood in this way:
"This person is indeed dissociated from the fetter of worldly material things and is intent upon the imperturbable.
Furthermore, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that some person here might be intent upon the base of nothingness.

For a person, Sunakkhatta, who is intent upon the base of nothingness, conversation appropriate to that state arises, and he reflects upon it and ponders it in accordance with its nature; he associates with such a person and finds satisfaction therein.

But when conversation connected with the imperturbable is being held, he does not wish to hear it, he does not lend an ear, he does not apply his mind to understand it, nor does he associate with such a person or find satisfaction therein.
"Just as, Sunakkhatta, a large stone split in two cannot be joined back together,
even so, Sunakkhatta, for a person who is intent upon the base of nothingness, those fetters of imperturbability are broken.
He should be understood in this way:"
‘Indeed, a person who is dissociated from the fetter of imperturbability is intent upon the base of nothingness.
Now, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that some person here might be intent upon the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For a person intent upon the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, Sunakkhatta, there is one who corresponds to that state.
When talk concerning the base of nothingness arises, he reflects upon it in accordance with its nature, ponders it, associates with the person who speaks it, and finds satisfaction in it;

yet when talk connected with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises, he does not wish to hear it, does not lend an ear, does not apply his mind to understand it, does not associate with that person, and does not find satisfaction in it.
“Suppose, Sunakkhatta, a man had eaten a delicious meal and then threw it away.
What do you think, Sunakkhatta,
would that man have any desire to eat that food again?”
“No, venerable sir.”—
“For what reason?”—
“Because that food, venerable sir, is considered repulsive.”
“In the same way, Sunakkhatta, for a person who is intent upon the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, those fetters belonging to the base of nothingness have been vomited out.
He should be understood thus:
‘This person, intent upon the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, is indeed dissociated from the fetter of the base of nothingness.’”
"It is indeed possible, Sunakkhatta, that here some person might be rightly intent upon Nibbāna.
For a person, Sunakkhatta, who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna, conversation appropriate to that state arises;
he reflects and ponders in accordance with that Dhamma; he associates with such a person and finds satisfaction therein."

Furthermore, when a discourse connected with the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is being delivered, he does not wish to hear it, he does not lend an ear, he does not apply his mind to understand it, he does not associate with that person, and he finds no satisfaction in it.
Just as, Sunakkhatta, a palm tree whose crown has been cut off is incapable of further growth; so too is this man.

In the same way, Sunakkhatta, for a person who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna, those fetters pertaining to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception have been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and are subject to non-arising in the future.
He should be understood thus:
‘This person, rightly intent upon Nibbāna, is indeed dissociated from the fetter of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’”
But it is possible, Sunakkhatta, that some bhikkhu here might think:
"Craving has been called an arrow by the Recluse; it is the poisonous humour of ignorance, and it is shattered by desire, lust, and ill will.
That arrow of craving has been abandoned by me; the poisonous humour of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna."
Thus he would have such [qualities] even though they are not real.
He would devote himself to those things that are unsuitable for one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna;

he would devote himself to seeing forms with the eye in an unsuitable way, he would devote himself to hearing sounds with the ear in an unsuitable way, he would devote himself to smelling odors with the nose in an unsuitable way...

One might devote oneself to an unsuitable scent with the nose; one might devote oneself to an unsuitable taste with the tongue; one might devote oneself to an unsuitable tangible object with the body;
one might devote oneself to an unsuitable mental phenomenon with the mind.
For one thus devoted to unsuitable seeing of forms with the eye, and devoted to unsuitable hearing of sounds with the ear...
If one who is devoted to an unsuitable odor with the nose, an unsuitable taste with the tongue,
an unsuitable tangible object with the body, or an unsuitable mental phenomenon with the mind,
lust would assail his heart. With a heart assailed by lust, he might meet death or suffering amounting to death.
"Just as if, Sunakkhatta, a man were pierced by an arrow smeared with a potent poison,
and his friends, companions, kinsmen, and relatives were to bring a physician and a surgeon for him;
and that physician and surgeon were to cut around the opening of the wound with a blade."
Having cut around the opening of the wound with a knife, one would search for the arrow with a probe.
Having searched for the arrow with the probe, one would extract the arrow and remove the poisonous matter along with its residue.
Knowing that there is still a residue, one would say this:
“O man, your arrow has been pulled out and the poisonous humor removed, though a residue remains.
There is no longer any obstacle for you.
You should eat only suitable food; do not eat unsuitable food, lest your wound begin to suppurate.”

“From time to time you should wash the wound; from time to time you should anoint the opening of the wound. Do not let pus and blood cover the opening of the wound because you have failed to wash it from time to time or to anoint its opening from time to time.
Do not subject yourself to wind and sun; do not let dust and grit infect the opening of the wound because you have subjected yourself to wind and sun.
And you should live, good man, protecting the wound and seeking its healing.”
It would occur to him:
“The arrow has been pulled out from me; the poisonous humor has been removed without remainder.
There is no longer any obstacle for me.”
Thus, he would eat foods that are unsuitable. As he eats those unsuitable foods, his wound would discharge.
He would not wash the wound from time to time, nor would he anoint the opening of the wound from time to time.
Because he does not wash the wound from time to time and does not anoint the opening of the wound from time to time, pus and blood would cover the opening of the wound.
And he would devote himself to walking in the wind and sun. While he was devoted to walking in the wind and sun, dust and grit would infect the opening of his wound.
He would neither protect the wound nor apply healing oil to it.
Because of this unwholesome practice, the impurity and toxic humors that had been removed but still left with a residue would, through both factors, cause the wound to become more extensive.
Just as a wound that has become suppurated might lead to death or to suffering amounting to death, even so, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might think:
“Craving has been called an arrow by the Recluse; the poison of ignorance is corrupted by desire, lust, and ill will.”
‘That arrow of craving has been abandoned by me; the poisonous humor of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna.
Such would be his conceit, even though it is not true.
He would devote himself to those things that are unsuitable for one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna, and he would [behave] unsuitably with the eye...
One might devote oneself to seeing forms; one might devote oneself to sounds that are unsuitable for the ear; one might devote oneself to odors that are unsuitable for the nose;
one might devote oneself to tastes that are unsuitable for the tongue; one might devote oneself to tangibles that are unsuitable for the body;
one might devote oneself to mental phenomena that are unsuitable for the mind.
If, while devoted to seeing forms with the eye that are unwholesome, devoted to hearing sounds with the ear that are unwholesome,
devoted to smelling odors with the nose that are unwholesome, devoted to tasting flavors with the tongue that are unwholesome,
devoted to touching tangibles with the body that are unwholesome, and devoted to cognizing mental phenomena with the mind that are unwholesome, lust should assail his mind.
Thus, with a mind not uprooted from lust, one might meet death or suffering equal to death.
For in the discipline of the Noble One, Sunakkhatta, he who renounces the training and reverts to the low life meets death;
and in the discipline of the Noble One, Sunakkhatta, he who commits any defiled offense meets suffering equal to death.
"It is indeed possible, Sunakkhatta, that some bhikkhu here might think:
‘Craving has been called a dart by the ascetic; the poisonous humour of ignorance is afflicted by desire, lust, and ill will.
That dart of craving has been abandoned by me; the poisonous humour of ignorance has been removed; I am one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna.’"
For one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna, he should not devote himself to those things that are unsuitable for one rightly intent upon Nibbāna;
he should not devote himself to unsuitable seeing of forms with the eye, he should not devote himself to unsuitable hearing of sounds with the ear,
he should not devote himself to unsuitable smelling of odors with the nose, he should not devote himself to unsuitable tasting of flavors with the tongue.
One should not devote oneself to an unwholesome tangible object with the body; one should not devote oneself to an unwholesome mental phenomenon with the mind.

For one who does not devote oneself to seeing an unwholesome form with the eye, who does not devote oneself to hearing an unwholesome sound with the ear, who does not devote oneself to smelling an unwholesome odor with the nose, who does not devote oneself to tasting an unwholesome flavor with the tongue... [and so forth].
For one who is not devoted to tactile objects with the body, nor to mental phenomena that are unsuitable with the mind, lust would not obsess the heart.
With a heart unobsessed by lust, he would neither meet death nor experience suffering equal to death.
Sunakkhatta, it is just as if a man were pierced by an arrow smeared with a potent poison.
His friends, companions, kinsmen, and blood relatives would have a physician and surgeon attend to him.
That physician and surgeon would cut open the opening of the wound with a knife;
having cut open the opening of the wound with a knife, he would search for the arrowhead with a probe.
Having sought out the arrow with a probe, one would extract the arrow and remove the poisonous humor without remainder.
Knowing that it was without remainder, he would say:
"O man, your arrow has been extracted; the poisonous humor has been removed without remainder."
And this shall not be an obstacle for you.
You should eat food that is wholesome; do not eat unwholesome food, lest the wound become suppurating.

You should wash the wound from time to time and anoint the opening of the wound from time to time. Do not let pus and blood cover the opening of the wound because you do not wash it from time to time nor anoint its opening from time to time.
"Do not devote yourself to walking in the wind and sun; lest, while you are devoted to walking in the wind and sun, dust and grit should infect the opening of your wound.
And so, good man, you should dwell protecting the wound and seeking the healing of the wound.
Then it would occur to him:
‘The arrow has been pulled out from me; the poisonous humor has been removed without remainder.
There is no longer anything to cause an obstruction for me.
He would then eat only suitable food. As he eats suitable food, his wound would not discharge pus.

From time to time he should wash the wound, and from time to time he should apply ointment to the opening of the wound. As he washes the wound from time to time and applies ointment to the opening of the wound from time to time, pus and blood will not cover the opening of the wound.
He should not expose himself to wind and sun. By not exposing himself to wind and sun, dust and grit will not infect the opening of the wound.
And he should live protecting the wound, seeking the healing of the wound.
If, through this beneficial practice and by the removal of that poisonous humor without remainder,
the wound were to heal— then, with the wound healed and the scab fallen away, he would incur neither death nor suffering amounting to death.
In the same way, Sunakkhatta, it is possible that a certain bhikkhu here might think thus:
‘Craving, indeed, has been called an arrow by the ascetic; the poisonous humor of ignorance is afflicted by desire, lust, and ill will.
That arrow of craving has been abandoned by me; the poisonous humor of ignorance has been removed;
I am one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna. While he is thus rightly intent upon Nibbāna, those things which are unsuitable for one who is rightly intent upon Nibbāna—those [he avoids].
One should not indulge in it; one should not indulge in seeing forms with the eye that are unsuitable; one should not indulge in hearing sounds with the ear that are unsuitable;
one should not indulge in smelling odors with the nose that are unsuitable; one should not indulge in tasting flavors with the tongue that are unsuitable;
one should not indulge in touching tangibles with the body that are unsuitable; one should not indulge in cognizing mental phenomena with the mind that are unsuitable.
If he does not indulge in what is unsuitable— seeing forms with the eye, hearing sounds with the ear,
smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue,
touching tangibles with the body, or cognizing mental phenomena with the mind— then lust will not overwhelm his mind.
Thus, with a mind not stirred by lust, one would neither meet death nor experience suffering equal to death.
This, Sunakkhatta, is a simile I have used to make the meaning clear;
this is the meaning here.
“Wound,” Sunakkhatta, is a designation for these six internal sense bases;
“poisonous humour,” Sunakkhatta, is a designation for ignorance;
and “dart,” Sunakkhatta, is a designation for craving.
"Seeking," Sunakkhatta, is a designation for mindfulness;
"the surgeon," Sunakkhatta, is a designation for noble wisdom;
"the physician, the remover of arrows," Sunakkhatta, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"So indeed, Sunakkhatta, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who acts with restraint regarding the six bases of contact, having understood:

'Acquisition is the root of suffering,' and being without acquisition, liberated through the destruction of acquisition, would either direct his body toward acquisition or give rise to a mind [clinging] to acquisition.
Just as, Sunakkhatta, there might be a bronze vessel for drinking water, endowed with beautiful color, fragrance, and flavor..."
And that [mixture] was mixed with poison.
Then a man might come along, desiring life, not desiring death, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering.
What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
“Would that man drink from that vessel of beverage if he knew:
‘Having drunk this, I shall meet death or suffer pain amounting to death’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“In the same way, Sunakkhatta, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has practiced restraint regarding the six bases of contact, having understood:

‘Acquisition is the root of suffering,’ and being without acquisition, liberated through the destruction of acquisition, would either direct his body toward acquisition or give rise to a mind [clinging] to acquisition. This is not possible.
It is just as if, Sunakkhatta, there were a venomous snake with terrible poison.”
Then suppose a man were to come along, desiring life, not desiring death, desiring happiness, and averse to suffering.
What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
Would that man give his hand or his thumb to that fierce-poisoned viper, knowing: [that it would bring him safety]?
“‘Bitten by this, I shall meet death or suffering amounting to death,’ would you say?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“In the same way, Sunakkhatta, that bhikkhu who practices restraint regarding the six bases of contact [thinks]: ‘Acquisition is the root of suffering.’”

"Having understood this, for one who is liberated through the destruction of the acquisitions (upadhisaṅkhaye) and is without acquisitions (nirupadhi), it is impossible that he would apply the body to the acquisitions or give rise to a [defiled] mind within the acquisitions.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The *Sunakkhatta Sutta*, the fifth, is finished.
